body.statement:
For every pair of integers \(n,k\geq 1\) and every rational \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfying
\[
\alpha_n(3T_k^\dagger+2\varepsilon)\leq 1,
\]
the corrected Airy-tube Bayes deficit at the zero-count allocation \((n,0,0)\) obeys
\[
G_{n,k,\varepsilon}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}(n,0,0)
\geq
\frac{11}{8}\int_{\mathbb R}|x|w_k^\dagger(x)\,dx
+\frac{45}{256}\varepsilon.
\]
Consequently, for every sequence \(k_n\to\infty\) and every positive sequence \(\varepsilon_n\) satisfying the displayed admissibility condition,
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
G_{n,k_n,\varepsilon_n}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}(n,0,0)
\geq \frac{22}{15}\Lambda_{c^\dagger}
>\Lambda_{c^\dagger}.
\]
In particular, there is no sequence \(e_{\mathrm{zero},n}\to0\) for which
\(G_{n,k_n,\varepsilon_n}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}(r)
\leq\Lambda_{c^\dagger}+e_{\mathrm{zero},n}\) holds for every zero-count allocation \(r\).
body.proof_tex:
Fix an admissible triple \((n,k,\varepsilon)\).  Conditional on the tube coordinates \((x,h)\), the operation ``draw a multinomial response-count vector and then draw a labeling uniformly in its orbit'' in \(\mathrm{def:explicit\text{-}three\text{-}arm\text{-}airy\text{-}tube}\) is exactly equivalent to drawing the labeled response types \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) independently with common law \(p_{n,x,h}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}\).  Indeed, for any labeled sequence with count vector \(m\), the multinomial mass is
\[
\frac{n!}{\prod_t m_t!}\prod_t
\bigl(p_{n,x,h,t}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}\bigr)^{m_t},
\]
and the reciprocal orbit size is \(\prod_t m_t!/n!\); their product is the independent-product mass.

Consider the deterministic, outcome-independent allocation having count vector \((n,0,0)\).  It reveals \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=t_{i,1}\) for every \(i\).  The estimator
\[
\widetilde\tau_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1)
\]
is measurable from these observations and lies in \([-1,1]\).  Write
\[
e(t)=2t_1-1-(c^\dagger)^\top t.
\]
The exact target identity in \(\mathrm{prop:unequal\text{-}three\text{-}arm\text{-}exact\text{-}primitives}\) gives
\[
\widetilde\tau_n-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e(t_i).
\]
The same proposition gives \(v_1=1/2\), \(d_1^\dagger=0\),
\(\mathbb E[b_t\mid x,h]=\alpha_n(xv+hd^\dagger)\), and
\(\mathbb E[(c^\dagger)^\top t\mid x,h]=\alpha_nx\).  Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[e(t)\mid x,h]
=2\alpha_n(xv_1+hd_1^\dagger)-\alpha_nx=0. \tag{1}
\]

In lexicographic order \(000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111\), direct substitution of
\(c^\dagger=(1,-1/4,-3/4)\) gives
\[
e(t)^2=left(1,\frac1{16},\frac9{16},0,0,
\frac9{16},\frac1{16},1\right). \tag{2}
\]
Hence \(\mathbb E_{p_0^\dagger}[e(t)^2]=1\).  Using the four response measures in
\(\mathrm{def:explicit\text{-}three\text{-}arm\text{-}airy\text{-}tube}\), equation (2) also gives, for either sign,
\[
\sum_t\lambda_{v,t}^{\pm}e(t)^2=\frac{13}{8},
\qquad
\sum_t\lambda_{d,t}^{\pm}e(t)^2=\frac{23}{16}.
\]
The longitudinal and transverse measures have respective total masses three and two.  Substitution in the defining formula for \(p_{n,x,h}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}\) therefore yields the exact identity
\[
\mathbb E[e(t)^2\mid x,h]
=1-\alpha_n\left(\frac{11}{8}|x|+
\frac9{16}|h|\right). \tag{3}
\]
The admissibility inequality makes \(p_{n,x,h}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}\) a probability law, so all the preceding conditional expectations are well defined.

By conditional independence, (1), and (3), the conditional squared-error risk of \(\widetilde\tau_n\) is
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[
(\widetilde\tau_n-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m))^2\mid x,h\right]
=\frac1n\left\{1-\alpha_n\left(
\frac{11}{8}|x|+\frac9{16}|h|\right)\right\}. \tag{4}
\]
The coordinates are independent with densities \(w_k^\dagger\) and \(\rho_\varepsilon\).  Direct integration of the stated polynomial density gives
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}|h|\rho_\varepsilon(h)\,dh
=\frac{30}{16\varepsilon}\int_0^\varepsilon
h\left(1-\frac{h^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)^2dh
=\frac{5}{16}\varepsilon. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(\alpha_n=n^{-1/3}\), averaging (4) and applying (5) shows that this particular estimator has Bayes risk
\[
\frac1n-n^{-4/3}\left\{
\frac{11}{8}\int_{\mathbb R}|x|w_k^\dagger(x)\,dx
+\frac{45}{256}\varepsilon\right\}. \tag{6}
\]
The posterior mean minimizes integrated squared error.  Thus the exact Bayes risk
\(\mathcal B_{n,k,\varepsilon}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}(n,0,0)\) defined in
\(\mathrm{def:exact\text{-}airy\text{-}tube\text{-}bayes\text{-}risk}\) is at most (6).  Rearranging its definition of \(G_{n,k,\varepsilon}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}\) proves the first displayed inequality of the lemma.

It remains to evaluate its limit.  Put \(\Phi=\phi_{c^\dagger}\),
\(A=\int_{\mathbb R}|\Phi'|^2\), and
\(B=\int_{\mathbb R}|x|\Phi^2\).  The scaled functions
\(\Phi_s(x)=s^{1/2}\Phi(sx)\), \(s>0\), have unit \(L^2\) norm and Airy energy
\[
4s^2A+\kappa(c^\dagger)s^{-1}B.
\]
Because \(\Phi\) is the ground-state minimizer specified in
\(\mathrm{def:airy\text{-}benchmark}\), this differentiable expression has derivative zero at \(s=1\).  Hence
\[
8A=\kappa(c^\dagger)B,
\qquad
\Lambda_{c^\dagger}=4A+\kappa(c^\dagger)B,
\qquad
B=\frac{2\Lambda_{c^\dagger}}{3\kappa(c^\dagger)}
=\frac{16}{15}\Lambda_{c^\dagger}, \tag{7}
\]
where the last equality uses the proved value \(\kappa(c^\dagger)=5/8\).

The weighted \(H^1\) convergence in
\(\mathrm{lem:effective\text{-}normalized\text{-}airy\text{-}record}\) implies both
\(\int(\varphi_k^\dagger)^2\to1\) and
\[
\int |x|\left|(\varphi_k^\dagger)^2-\Phi^2\right|
\leq
\left(\int |x||\varphi_k^\dagger-\Phi|^2\right)^{1/2}
\left(\int |x||\varphi_k^\dagger+\Phi|^2\right)^{1/2}
\longrightarrow0. \tag{8}
\]
The second factor in (8) is bounded because of the same weighted convergence.  By the definition
\(w_k^\dagger=(\varphi_k^\dagger)^2/\int(\varphi_k^\dagger)^2\), equations (7)--(8) give
\[
\int |x|w_k^\dagger(x)\,dx\longrightarrow
\frac{16}{15}\Lambda_{c^\dagger}.
\]
The nonnegative transverse term may be discarded.  Therefore every sequence in the lemma satisfies
\[
\liminf_nG_{n,k_n,\varepsilon_n}^{\dagger,\mathrm A}(n,0,0)
\geq \frac{11}{8}\frac{16}{15}\Lambda_{c^\dagger}
=\frac{22}{15}\Lambda_{c^\dagger}.
\]
Positivity of \(\Lambda_{c^\dagger}\) makes this strictly larger than
\(\Lambda_{c^\dagger}\).  Since \((n,0,0)\) is itself a zero-count allocation, any purported uniform zero-face error must have lower limit at least
\(7\Lambda_{c^\dagger}/15\), proving the final assertion.
